title: Orchestrator → Runtime Handoff Procedures and Region Zoning
content:
Purpose:
This note captures a concrete, operational handoff pattern between the control-plane orchestrator (region-aware) and the various runtime adapters (GPU pools, VPC runtimes, edge nodes). The intent is to document step-by-step responsibilities, error handling, and routing policy semantics per region/zone so teams have an actionable playbook for rollouts and incident triage.

Context / why this matters:
- We increasingly route requests by latency SLOs, cost tier, and data residency. The orchestrator needs to make deterministic decisions and provide clear contracts for runtime adapters to accept or reject work.
- Current gaps: unclear retry semantics across regions, inconsistent metadata on handoff, and ambiguous ownership during adapter failover.

High-level goals:
- Define a minimal, reliable handoff RPC with explicit outcome states (ACCEPTED / QUEUED / DECLINED / ERROR) and durable trace IDs.
- Ensure region zoning rules are declarative and versioned (so rollout can change behavior without runtime code changes).
- Codify who owns each failure mode and the preferred remediation path.

Terminology (used in examples):
- Orchestrator: control-plane component that selects target runtime adapters and issues the handoff.
- Runtime adapter: service responsible for translating handoff requests into local runtime actions (GPU scheduler, autoscaler, local cache).
- Zone: a logical routing region (e.g., us-west-1-primary, eu-west-1-secondary) composed of one or more adapter clusters.
- Handoff Envelope: JSON payload with trace_id, client_metadata, model_spec, routing_constraints, cost_tier_hint, and ttl.

Handoff RPC contract (v1):
- Endpoint: POST /v1/handoff
- Required headers: X-Trace-Id, X-Orchestrator-Version, X-Requested-At
- Body: Handoff Envelope (see example below)
- Expected responses:
  - 202 ACCEPTED {status: "ACCEPTED", runtime_id: "r-123", provisionETA_ms: 0}
  - 202 QUEUED {status: "QUEUED", queue_pos: 4, estimate_ms: 450}
  - 409 DECLINED {status: "DECLINED", reason: "model-not-supported"}
  - 500 ERROR {status: "ERROR", code: "adapter-timeout"}
- Invariants:
  - If ACCEPTED returned, orchestrator marks request as routed and starts per-token timeout monitoring.
  - If QUEUED, orchestrator attaches a watcher with exponential backoff but maximum total wait = Handoff Envelope.ttl.
  - If DECLINED, orchestrator must attempt fallback policy (regional variant, lower cost-tier model) unless the policy explicitly prohibits fallback.

Handoff Envelope example (stringified JSON in body):
{
  "trace_id": "trace-20241107-xyz",
  "client": {"org": "acme", "project": "chat-prod"},
  "model_spec": {"name": "redwood-7b-quant", "version": "v2"},
  "routing_constraints": {"region_preferences": ["eu-west-1","eu-west-2"], "latency_slo_ms": 150},
  "cost_tier_hint": "balanced",
  "ttl_ms": 120000
}

Region Zoning & Policy primitives:
- Zone definitions are stored in a declarative policy repo (git) and referenced by orchestrator via a config hash. Example zone policies:
  - eu-west-1-primary: prefer local adapters, allow eu-west-2 fallback, enforce data-residency:true
  - us-west-1-burst: permit bursting to shared-dedicated when cost_tier_hint != "low"
- Policy primitives exposed to orchestrator:
  - affinity: strong | soft | none
  - fallback_order: ordered list of zones/adapters
  - runtime_compat: list of supported model families / quantization profiles
  - enforcement: best-effort | strict (strict blocks cross-region fallback)

Ownership matrix (concise):
- Orchestrator team (eng-platform-engineering): decides routing policy versions, orchestrator-initiated timeouts, and global fallback policy. Responsible for: config versioning, rollout, observability hooks (trace annotations).
- Runtime adapters (serving-runtime + private-deployments): own adapter-side admission (ACCEPT/QUEUE/DECLINE), provisioning ETA accuracy, local autoscale signals, and per-adapter health semantics.
- SRE: owns cross-region failover playbooks, incident runbooks for cross-zone blackholes, and on-call for region-wide advisories.

Failure modes and remediation (owner callouts):
- adapter-timeout (adapter fails to respond within X ms): Orchestrator retries once to next candidate, increments metric handoff.adapter_timeouts. Owner: orchestrator.
- model-not-supported: Adapter returns DECLINED with reason; Orchestrator consults policy fallback_order and tries next compatible adapter. Owner: serving-runtime must update runtime_compat lists in policy repo.
- slow-queue-growth: Adapter reports persistent QUEUED with rising queue_pos; SRE alert if queue_pos > 50 for > 5m. Orchestrator can trigger overflow to burst pools. Owner: SRE + orchestrator co-owned.
- cross-region-violation (adapter accepted when strict enforcement policy forbids it): Audit alert and rollback to prior policy version. Owner: platform-engineering + security/compliance.

Observability hooks (must be present in v1):
- Trace annotations: handoff.sent_at, handoff.adapter_id, handoff.outcome, handoff.retries, zone_policy_hash.
- Metrics: handoff.latency_ms (P50/P95/P99), handoff.outcome_counts, adapter.queue_length, adapter.provision_eta_ms.
- Logs: structured json with trace_id, model_spec, client.owner, decision_path (why this adapter was picked).

Region-aware rollout recipe (for policy changes):
1) Author new zone policy in git repo (policy branch).
2) Create canary release: orchestrator reads new policy hash but only applies to 2% of traffic in non-critical zones.
3) Monitor handoff.metrics for 30m: compare adapter rejections, queue rates, latency.
4) If regressions, revert policy hash; if healthy, increase to 20% then 100% over 6–12 hours.
5) Record rollout in change log with link to PR and metrics snapshot.

Operational examples (short):
- Scenario A: eu-west-1 outage
  - Orchestrator detects adapter cluster unhealthy via health API. Policy fallback_order sends traffic to eu-west-2-secondary. Orchestrator annotates traces with reason: "cluster-health-failed". SRE runbook page: confluence.redwood/sre/region-eu-west-outage
- Scenario B: sudden spike in burst pool cost
  - Billing alert triggers automated policy shift: orchestrator reduces cost_tier_hint allowed for burst pools and favors local queues. Ticket: JIRA-PLAT-1987

Open questions / follow-ups:
- Should adapters be allowed to return a suggested_fallback_id with DECLINED? (helps orchestrator pick next candidate without extra lookups). Action: prototype in PLAT-1423.
- TTL enforcement: should orchestrator enforce global hard ttl, or allow adapter to extend queue TTL? Risk: unbounded latency. Recommendation: orchestrator enforces hard ttl; adapter can return estimated wait but cannot extend beyond envelope.ttl.
- Backpressure signals: standardize a small set of backpressure codes (RATE_LIMIT, CPU_HELD, MEM_PRESSURE, QUEUE_FULL). Add to adapter API v2.

Appendix: quick checklist for adapter owners (pre-deploy):
- implement /v1/handoff endpoint; return defined statuses
- emit trace annotations and standard metrics
- document runtime_compat and keep policy repo updated
- provide a small health summary endpoint for orchestrator to check (healthy | degraded | unreachable)

Notes to reviewers:
- This is intentionally pragmatic and conservative — aim for a small, testable RPC surface first.
- Feedbacks: please add missing failure modes and any company-specific compliance constraints (data residency enforcement examples).

Last edited by Aisha Patel on 2025-01-12.
